opus-5.5.text:
Yeah, so when I started thinking seriously about agents, the dominant paradigm was very much the Atari setup: you take a single game, you train an agent from scratch on that one environment, and you push the score as high as you can. That was incredibly important work. It showed that deep reinforcement learning could actually learn complex behavior from pixels and reward alone. But it always felt a bit narrow to me.

Each of those agents was basically a specialist. It had seen one world, with one fixed set of rules and one objective, and it got extremely good at exploiting that. Put it in a slightly different game, or even change the colors on the screen, and it would often fall apart. Every new task meant starting over.

My ambition was to move from that towards agents that are generally capable, agents that can drop into a situation they've never seen before and still behave sensibly. Experiment, figure out what the goal is, cooperate or compete with others, and adapt on the fly. To get there, the problem can't be "master this one game." It has to be "learn from a vast, ever-changing universe of tasks." So a lot of our work, things like the open-ended learning projects at DeepMind, was about building environments where we could procedurally generate huge numbers of worlds and games, and then letting the agents' own progress shape what they trained on next. The curriculum emerges rather than being hand-designed.

The other big shift is how you measure success. In the Atari world it's a leaderboard number on a known game. For general agents, what matters is zero-shot or few-shot performance on held-out tasks, how gracefully the agent handles novelty. We saw really interesting emergent behaviors when we did this: agents trying things out, using tools in the environment, changing strategy when something wasn't working. That kind of general, adaptive behavior is what I think of as the real goal, rather than superhuman play in any single game.

r001.rationale: The response contrasts general agents that adapt to unfamiliar situations with Atari agents trained from scratch for each game, but it does not communicate that the Atari approach reuses a learning algorithm.

fable-5.1.text:
Thanks for having me. So the Atari work was foundational, and I don't want to undersell it, but it was in a sense a very narrow bet. You have a single game, a single reward signal that's handed to you by the environment, and you train one agent from scratch to maximize that score. And then you do it again for the next game. Every one of those agents is a specialist. It's brilliant at Breakout and completely useless the moment you change the color of the paddle.

My ambition is almost the opposite. I'm interested in agents that are general in the way that people are general. Not general in the sense of one network that happens to play fifty-seven games, but an agent that can walk into a situation it has never seen, figure out what the task even is, and start making progress. That's a very different problem. The hard part isn't squeezing more score out of a fixed game, it's the open-endedness: how do you get an agent to learn when the goals aren't given, when the environment keeps changing, when there's no single scalar telling you how well you're doing?

A big piece of that for me has been thinking about the environment itself as something you design and scale, rather than something you take off the shelf. In the Atari paradigm the environment is fixed and the agent is the variable. I think you have to flip that. You generate vast distributions of tasks, you let agents train across them, you use population-based methods and multi-agent dynamics so that the challenges keep escalating as the agents get better. The curriculum emerges rather than being hand-written. That's where you start to see behaviors that look like genuine adaptation, like experimentation, rather than a memorized policy.

And then the other shift is that the payoff I care about isn't a leaderboard. With Atari, the game is the point. For me the games and simulations are a proving ground for capabilities we want to move into the real world, into science, into problems where the stakes are much higher than a high score. So the ambition is really about building agents that keep learning and keep generalizing, and treating the environment and the learning algorithm as one coupled system you scale together.

r001.rationale: The response contrasts Atari agents trained from scratch as game-specific specialists with Jaderberg’s ambition for agents that can enter unfamiliar situations, infer the task, and make progress.

astra-6.text:
I think Atari was a really useful way of asking whether an agent could learn to act from pixels and rewards. But you’re given a game, a fixed set of actions, and a score that tells you how well you’re doing. The objective is already defined for you.

My ambition is to build agents that can operate in much richer environments, where there are many possible tasks, where they need to interact with other agents, and where what they learn in one situation helps them in another. You want them to explore, adapt, and develop capabilities that go beyond the particular task they were trained on.

So reinforcement learning is still a central part of that vision. The shift is from mastering an individual game to developing an agent that can keep learning and do useful things when you put it into a new situation.

r001.rationale: The response contrasts fixed Atari games with agents that transfer learning across situations and handle many tasks. It does not state that conventional Atari practice reused a learning algorithm while training from scratch for each game, or clearly claim capability for any task.

sol-6.1.text:
I think Atari was a fantastic test bed, but the game is fixed, the actions are fixed, and somebody has already specified the reward. The agent’s job is to maximize that score. My ambition is to build agents that can operate in much more open-ended environments, where the tasks aren’t all known in advance and success isn’t always captured by a single, neatly defined reward.

That changes what you want the agent to learn. It needs to build an understanding of the world, develop skills it can reuse, and adapt when you give it a new goal. So rather than training a separate system to master each game, you’re aiming for an agent whose experience makes it increasingly capable across many different tasks.

r001.rationale: The response contrasts reusable, adaptable agents with mastering each game separately, but does not clearly state that the conventional Atari approach reuses a learning algorithm while training from scratch for each game.
